newsitem.title: USA: Clinton warns America risks return to segregation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton warns America risks return to segregation.

text.p: President Bill Clinton warned on Saturday that the United States is showing signs of a return to racial segregation more than 30 years after the civil rights revolution, and he said: "America cannot make that mistake again."

"We have torn down the barriers in our laws. Now we must break down the barriers in our lives, our minds and our hearts," he said in excerpts of a widely anticipated speech prepared for delivery at the commencement ceremony for the University of California at San Diego.

A son of the South who witnessed the civil rights upheavals of the 1960s, Clinton used his commencement address to launch a year-long look at the race issue. He acknowledged that "history reminds us that it will be hard" to breach the racial divide.

He said a sign of a return to segregation was heralded by California's approval last year of Proposition 209, which ordered the repeal of affirmative action programmes granting preferences to minorities on government hiring and student acceptance within the state's university system.
The effect of the decision, he said, has been "dramatic and devastating" because it prompted minority enrollments in law school and other graduate programmes to plummet for the first time in decades.
"Some of the brightest students won't even apply, they feel so unwelcome. Soon the same will likely happen in college. Call it what you will -- but I call it resegregation.

"I have seen the damage segregation brought to my native South. America cannot make that mistake again," said Clinton, who as an 11-year-old watched the forced integration of Little Rock Central High School in his home state of Arkansas.

With Clinton were the seven members of an advisory board he appointed on Thursday to conduct town hall meetings, examine the state of race relations in the country and in a year give Americans a report outlining "facts, not myths" about the problems and ways to solve them.
The initiative comes at a time when many black Americans feel they are being left behind in the country's economic good times, their communities ravaged by bloodshed, crime and drugs.

At the same time some whites feel government policies giving minorities preferences on hiring and education are edging them out. To the distress of minorities, these so-called affirmative action programmes are increasingly under fire. California's vote to eliminate them is being fought by the Clinton administration in court.

Attending the speech was Ward Connerly, the chief advocate of Proposition 209. He ran radio ads attacking Clinton's speech even before the president arrived to deliver it. He was attending by virtue of being a regent of the university.
Clinton said Americans face a choice more than 30 years after the civil rights revolution led to a description of the country as "two Americans, one black, one white, separate and unequal."

"We will become not two, but many Americas, separate, unequal and isolated? Or will we draw strength from all our people and our ancient faith in equality and human dignity, to become the world's first truly multiracial democracy?" Clinton said.
"That is the unfinished work of our times: to lift the burden of race, and redeem the promise of America," he said.

A Gallup Poll this week found persistent gaps in attitudes and perceptions between blacks and whites. For example it said whites characterise themselves as having very little personal prejudice against blacks, but blacks feel whites have higher levels of racial prejudice than whites believe about themselves.

There is no doubt that racism remains a pervasive force in many parts of America. The Ku Klux Klan still burns crosses in the South. Even John Hope Franklin, 82-year-old chairman of the new advisory panel, said recently that, "We have a slave mentality working in this country. I am still called 'boy' sometimes."

Clinton sees now as the time to address the issue because of projections that by the year 2050, the minority population of the United States will rise to total 47 percent and the white majority narrowed to 53 percent.
Civil rights leaders who have been sceptical of the president's commitment to improving the lives of black Americans were waiting to hear what specific proposals Clinton will have in his remarks.
Clinton would like to make bridging the racial gap a lasting legacy of his presidency, to succeed where others have failed.
